questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Moment in Time When a Particle is Stationary
questions.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}-6t+10),\,t\ge 0.
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}-6t+10)) \\  & =\frac{2t-6}{{t}^{2}-6t+10} \\  & =\frac{2(t-3)}{{t}^{2}-6t+10}\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m/s}.$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2(t-3)}{{t}^{2}-6t+10} & =0 \\ 2(t-3) & =0 \\ t & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=3\,\text{s}.$

questions.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)=(t-3){e}^{t},\,t\ge 0.
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((t-3){e}^{t}) \\  & ={e}^{t}+(t-3){e}^{t} \\  & =(t-2){e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m/s}.$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(t-2){e}^{t} & =0 \\ t-2 & =0 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=2\,\text{s}.$

questions.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle at time $t$ is given by 

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}-2t+8,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Calculate the time when the particle is stationary, and give the displacement of the particle from the origin at this time.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t+8) \\  & =2t-2\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2t-2 & =0 \\ 2t & =2 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So the particle is stationary only at $t=1.$ To find the displacement from the origin at this time, we substitute $t=1$ back into $s(t)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}s(1) & ={1}^{2}-2(1)+8 \\  & =1-2+8 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=1$ and its displacement from the origin at this time is $7.$

questions.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t \\  & =t(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m/s}.$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1) & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1 & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-1/2} \\ t & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\,\text{s}.$

questions.problem: The displacement $s$ (in meters) relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=(4t-7){e}^{t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive.

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((4t-7){e}^{t}) \\  & =(4t-3){e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve $v(t)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & >0 \\ (4t-3){e}^{t} & >0 \\ 4t-3 & >0 \\ t & >\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing $x$ is $(\frac{3}{4},\infty ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6}) \\  & =(2t-4){e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we must solve $v(t)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ (2t-4){e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6} & <0 \\ 2t-4 & <0 \\ 2t & <4 \\ t & <2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $[0,2).$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=\frac{{t}^{3}}{2}-6{t}^{2}+30t+4,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{3}}{2}-6{t}^{2}+30t+4) \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}-12t+30\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}-12t+30) \\  & =3t-12\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}3t-12 & =0 \\ 3t & =12 \\ t & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the acceleration is zero when $t=4.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(4) & =\frac{3(4)^{2}}{2}-12(4)+30 \\  & =24-48+30 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=-\frac{2}{9}{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+14t+17,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2}{9}{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+14t+17) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{2}+6t+14\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{2}+6t+14) \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}t+6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{4}{3}t+6 \\ \frac{4}{3}t & =6 \\ t & =4.5\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=4.5.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
v(4.5)=-\frac{2}{3}(4.5)^{2}+6(4.5)+14=27.5.
$$

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t),\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+t\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t={e}^{-3/2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v({e}^{-3/2}) & =2({e}^{-3/2})\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-3/2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =2{e}^{-3/2}(-\frac{3}{2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =-2{e}^{-3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}-18t+3) \\  & =12t-18\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}12t-18 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{18}{12} \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t) = -\frac{1}{3}t^3 + \frac{5}{2}t^2 + 6t + 1,\quad t\geq 0.
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary, and give the displacement of the particle from the origin at this time.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{5}{2}{t}^{2}+6t+1) \\  & =-{t}^{2}+5t+6\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\, \textrm{m/s}$. So, we set $v = 0$ and solve for $t \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-{t}^{2}+5t+6 \\ 0 & ={t}^{2}-5t-6 \\ 0 & =(t-6)(t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $t=6$ and $t=-1.$ Since $t\geq 0,$ we discard the solution $t=-1$ and keep only $t=6.$

So the particle is stationary only at $t=6\, \textrm{s}.$ To find the displacement from the origin at this time, we substitute $t=6$ back into $s(t)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}s(6) & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {6}^{3}+\frac{5}{2}\cdot {6}^{2}+6\cdot 6+1 \\  & =-72+90+36+1 \\  & =55\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t = 6\, \textrm{s}$ and its displacement from the origin at this time is $55\, \textrm{m}.$
